front_blocks.md: What is an ion?

back_blocks.md: An ion is an electrically charged atom (or group of atoms) formed by the loss or gain of electrons. Positive ions (**cations**) form when atoms lose electrons; negative ions (**anions**) form when atoms gain electrons.

cards.front_md: What is an ion?
cards.back_md: An ion is an electrically charged atom (or group of atoms) formed by the loss or gain of electrons. Positive ions (**cations**) form when atoms lose electrons; negative ions (**anions**) form when atoms gain electrons.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Metals form negative ions by gaining electrons.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
Metals lose electrons to form positive ions (cations). Non-metals gain electrons to form negative ions (anions).

front_blocks.md: When sodium reacts with chlorine, sodium **..........**  one electron to form a **..........**  ion (Na<sup>+</sup>), while chlorine **..........**  one electron to form a negatively charged chloride ion (Cl<sup>-</sup>).

back_blocks.md: When sodium reacts with chlorine, sodium **loses** one electron to form a **positive** ion (Na<sup>+</sup>), while chlorine **gains** one electron to form a negatively charged chloride ion (Cl<sup>-</sup>).

front_blocks.md: Why do atoms form ions?

back_blocks.md: Atoms form ions by losing or gaining electrons to achieve a **full outer shell** of electrons, giving them the stable electronic configuration of a noble gas. This makes them more stable.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
The ionic bond is the electrostatic force of attraction between oppositely charged ions.

back_blocks.md: **True.**
Positive and negative ions are held together by strong electrostatic forces of attraction between their opposite charges. This force is called an ionic bond.

front_blocks.md: What charge do Group II elements form when they become ions, and why?

back_blocks.md: Group II elements form ions with a **2+** charge. They have 2 electrons in their outer shell and lose both to achieve a full outer shell, leaving them with 2 more protons than electrons.

back_blocks.md: Elements in Group 1 form ions with a **1+** charge, while elements in Group 7 form ions with a **1−** charge.

front_blocks.md: Describe the structure of an ionic compound.

back_blocks.md: Ionic compounds have a **giant lattice structure**: a regular, repeating arrangement of alternating positive and negative ions held together by **strong electrostatic forces** of attraction in all directions.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
In an ionic lattice, positive ions are only attracted to the nearest negative ions.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
In a giant ionic lattice, electrostatic forces act between oppositely charged ions **in all directions** throughout the structure, not just between nearest neighbours.

front_blocks.md: In magnesium oxide, magnesium loses **..........** electrons to form a **..........** ion, while oxygen gains **..........** electrons to form a 2- ion.

back_blocks.md: In magnesium oxide, magnesium loses **2** electrons to form a **2+** ion, while oxygen gains **2** electrons to form a 2- ion.

front_blocks.md: Why does an ionic compound have no overall charge?

back_blocks.md: In an ionic compound, the **total positive charge equals the total negative charge**, so they cancel out.
For example, in MgO, one Mg<sup>2+</sup> ion balances exactly one O<sup>2-</sup> ion, giving no overall charge.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Ionic compounds are formed when metal atoms react with non-metal atoms.

back_blocks.md: **True.**
Metal atoms **lose electrons** and non-metal atoms **gain them**, forming positive and negative ions. These attract each other to create the ionic compound.

front_blocks.md: In a dot-and-cross diagram of an ionic compound, what must you include around each ion?

back_blocks.md: Each ion must be enclosed in **square brackets** with the **ionic charge** written as a superscript outside the bracket. Only the outer shell electrons need to be shown, with dots representing electrons from one atom and crosses from the other.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Ionic compounds have high melting points because they contain strong covalent bonds.

back_blocks.md: **False.**

Ionic compounds have high melting points because of **strong electrostatic forces** of attraction between oppositely charged ions throughout the giant lattice. A large amount of energy is needed to overcome these forces.

front_blocks.md: Why do ionic compounds not conduct electricity in the solid state?

back_blocks.md: In a solid ionic compound, ions are held in **fixed positions** within the giant lattice. They **cannot move**, so there are no mobile charged particles to carry an electric current.

front_blocks.md: How does the charge on the ions in an ionic compound affect its melting point?

back_blocks.md: The **greater the charge** on the ions, the stronger the electrostatic forces of attraction and the **higher the melting point**. For example, MgO (Mg<sup>2+</sup> and O<sup>2-</sup>) has a higher melting point than NaCl (Na<sup>+</sup> and Cl<sup>-</sup>).

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
All ionic compounds are solid at room temperature.

back_blocks.md: **True.**
Ionic compounds have **high melting points** due to the strong electrostatic forces in their giant lattice structures, so they are all solid at room temperature.

front_blocks.md: Why does magnesium oxide have a higher melting point than sodium chloride?

back_blocks.md: Magnesium oxide contains **Mg**<sup>**2+**</sup>** and O**<sup>**2-**</sup>** ions**, which carry **greater charges** than the Na<sup>+</sup> and Cl<sup>-</sup> ions in sodium chloride. The stronger the charge on the ions, the stronger the electrostatic forces and the more energy needed to overcome them.
